core.p: **Part (b)**: In this extract Lady Macbeth is presented as a powerful woman. Explain how Lady Macbeth is presented **elsewhere in the play**. In your answer you must consider: how she is presented; the reasons she behaves as she does. You should refer to the context of the play. (20 marks)

bullets: **Thesis**: Lady Macbeth seizes the masculine power her society denies her by rejecting her nature, but Shakespeare shows that nature reasserts itself, so her collapse both evokes pity and reaffirms the Jacobean natural order.
**P2** 1.7 and 2.2: manipulation of manhood; control; first crack.
**P4** 5.1 and 5.9: sleepwalking; ‘fiend-like queen’ vs the audience’s pity.

essays.q: Explain how Lady Macbeth is presented elsewhere in the play.
essays.t: Model essay: Lady Macbeth and gender
essays.text:
Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a woman who tries to seize power by rejecting the femininity her society demanded; yet by tracing her from ‘unsex me here’ to ‘Out, damned spot!’, he shows that nature and conscience cannot be overturned, turning a figure of terror into one of pity.

In Act 1 Scene 5, Lady Macbeth’s first response to the prophecy is to fear her husband’s ‘milk of human kindness’; she associates gentleness with the maternal and therefore with weakness. Her soliloquy is an invocation: ‘Come, you spirits / That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here’. The imperative verbs and the summoning of spirits would sound to a Jacobean audience like witchcraft, which King James had written about in Daemonologie and which was punishable by death. She wishes to exchange her ‘milk for gall’, inverting the most natural female role, motherhood. Shakespeare shows that in a patriarchal society where women could not hold power directly, she can only gain it through her husband and by abandoning what her culture saw as her nature.

She uses this power through language. In Act 1 Scene 7, when Macbeth decides to ‘proceed no further’, she attacks his masculinity: ‘When you durst do it, then you were a man’. Her horrifying claim that she would have ‘dashed the brains out’ of her own baby rather than break a promise shocks him into agreement, and her confident ‘screw your courage to the sticking-place’ shows her command. Yet Shakespeare plants a crack. In Act 2 Scene 2 she admits she could not kill Duncan herself because he ‘resembled / My father as he slept’. The unsexing has not worked: family feeling and conscience survive beneath the performance.

As Macbeth’s power grows, hers fades. In Act 3 Scene 2 she reflects alone that ‘Nought’s had, all’s spent’, the monosyllables conveying exhausted disappointment, and Macbeth shuts her out of his plans: ‘Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck’. The affectionate ‘chuck’ is patronising; she has been returned to the passive role she tried to escape. At the banquet she again asks, ‘Are you a man?’, but the strategy that worked in Act 1 now fails, and she can only dismiss the guests. Shakespeare structures their relationship as a reversal: the partner who led becomes the wife who is excluded.

Her final scene completes the reversal. Sleepwalking, she speaks in fragmented prose rather than verse, and her imperatives now command an imaginary stain: ‘Out, damned spot! Out, I say!’ The woman who once said ‘A little water clears us of this deed’ now believes ‘all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand’; the diminutive ‘little’ reveals a vulnerability she once denied. She, who called on ‘thick night’, now insists on having a light by her at all times. The Doctor’s verdict, ‘More needs she the divine than the physician’, frames her illness as spiritual. Malcolm’s final label, ‘fiend-like queen’, gives the official Jacobean judgement of a woman who defied her place, but Shakespeare has shown the audience more: a woman broken by the guilt she tried to suppress. Her fate warns against overturning the natural order, yet it also asks us to pity her.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a woman who tries to seize power by rejecting the femininity her society demanded, but by tracing her collapse from ‘unsex me here’ to ‘Out, damned spot!’, he shows that nature and conscience cannot be overturned, turning a figure of terror into one of pity.
why: **AO1**: a developed, conceptual argument across the whole play with apt quotations.
**AO3**: patriarchy, witchcraft, Daemonologie, gender roles, used to explain her choices.
Final evaluation balances the official verdict with audience response.

model: Lady Macduff: natural mother, innocent, ‘I have done no harm’
Shakespeare contrasts two models of womanhood
Both are victims of Macbeth’s ambition in different ways
exam.q: Practice: write a paragraph comparing Lady Macbeth with Lady Macduff.
exam.tip: Lady Macduff is a foil: use her for range.

mistakes.r: Say her language resembles witchcraft; she is not a witch.
mistakes.w: Calling Lady Macbeth one of the Witches.

mistakes.r: Track her across the play: her change is the point.

summary: A full grade 9 part (b) model essay on Lady Macbeth and gender, tracing her from her invocation of the spirits to her sleepwalking, with Jacobean context on women, witchcraft and the natural order.
